In this lesson, you will begin to learn the fundamentals of programming a PLC. This lesson and the lessons to follow will fully describe the function, purpose, and usage of the PLC instruction set...
PLCs use a variety of different instructions to perform a multitude of tasks. Bit instructions are one type of instruction used by a PLC.
In this lesson, we will look at the details of bit instructions. By understanding bit instructions, you will find it easier to understand other more advanced instructions.
Let's begin the lesson on BIT INSTRUCTIONS................................
LESSON MENU
BIT INSTRUCTIONSTLE
Bit instructions are commonly used instructions in PLC programming. As their name indicates, they are used to perform operations dealing with a single bit of data.

Before looking at the actual bit instructions, let's review the operation of a ladder logic program. Below is an example of a ladder logic program.

The PLC begins at the top most rung and reads from left to right. Each rung may contain one or more test instructions and one or more operations. Test instructions are used to make decisions based on different conditions in the system....

Depending on the way the test instructions are used, rungs can require all conditions to be met before an operation is performed, or at least one of many conditions. The example below illustrates these types of configurations...
If the conditions are all met for that particular rung, one or more operation instructions can be evaluated. An operation could be used to turn off a motor, turn on a light, etc.

If the conditions are not met, the PLC processor continues to the next rung, ignoring the previous rung's operations. Once the processor has reached the end of the last rung, it begins again at the top...
Bit instructions are used for testing conditions and for performing operations. We will look at both cases while learning all of the bit instructions.
OSROSRhot raising OSRising OSRising OSRaising OSRising OSR
The instruction shown below is the eXamine If Closed (XIC) instruction. This instruction returns either true or false depending on the bit it is analyzing.

The bit to look at must be specified to the instruction. Normally, the bit is specified by an IO module, the word in that module, and then the bit of that word. Below is an example of this type of specification...

When the processor evaluates this instruction, it looks at the specified bit. If the bit being examined is high (referred to as the closed state), the XIC instruction returns true. If the bit is low, or opened, the XIC instruction returns false...
The next instruction we are going to look at is the eXamine If Open (XIO) instruction. This instruction is very similar to the XIC instruction.

Like the XIC instruction, the XIO instruction requires a specified bit, but the instruction operation is opposite. The XIO instruction returns a false for a high (closed) condition and a true for a low (open) condition...
These instructions are referred to as complements of one another. In other words, they provide exactly the opposite return values for the same input data.
The instruction shown below is the OuTput Energize (OTE) instruction. This instruction is used to set high (close) an output bit. This bit corresponds to an output connection of an output device...

The OTE command is dependent on the result of test instructions with the same rung. If the rung test instructions return true, the output bit is set high. If the test instructions return false, the output is not modified...
Below are two examples of using the OuTput Energize instruction. Notice that the test conditions are only true if you can draw a line from the beginning of the rung to the operation instruction.....

The line continues until a false condition is found. If there is a false condition, another path on the rung needs to be examined if possible. Once all paths have been tested and no path to the operation can be drawn, the condition is considered false...
The next instruction we are going to look at is the OuTput Latch (OTL) instruction. This instruction is used to set a bit high. However, this instruction cannot set a bit low.
OTLOTEIC
The OTL instruction is also considered an operation instruction. The operation of this instruction is dependent on the condition of rung logic before this instruction is analyzed.

If a true is returned by the test instructions, then the particular bit pointed to by the OTL instruction is set high, unless it is already high. If the test instructions return false, the bit remains unchanged...

This instruction is normally used to set output bits; however, it can also be used to set any bit data to one. This is very useful when you are initializing data and need to set a particular bit to one...
The complement to the OTL instruction is the OuTput Unlatch (OTU) instruction. This instruction is used to set a particular bit to low.

Just as with the OTL instruction, the OTU instruction requires the test logic to be true before it will unlatch the bit specified to the instruction. If the test logic returns false, the bit remains unchanged...

This instruction can also be used when initializing data to set particular bits to zero. It is important to note that the OTL and OTU instructions are normally used together to provide complete control over an output bit...
The last instruction we are going to look at is the One-Shot Rising (OSR) instruction. This instruction is much different than the ones you have learned about so far.

This instruction waits until the preceding test instructions go from low to high. A low to high transition is known as a rise. For this reason, this instruction requires memory to perform its function...

The OSR function requires 1 bit of storage. This bit should not be used for anything else. If you used this bit for other data storage in your programs, errors could occur from incorrect values being stored in the bit...
Initially, the bit is set to zero. When a false to true ( ) transition occurs on the preceding test instructions, the OSR bit goes high and the operations after the OSR bit are performed..

When the processor cycles through the ladder logic program and back to this instruction, the bit is reset to zero. The OSR instruction now waits for another low to high transition before allowing the operation after it in the rung...
It is important to note that this instruction only allows the operations to occur once per transition. This is referred to as the "one-shot".
In this lesson, we have examined the bit instructions common to most PLC systems. In some cases, the mnemonics and names may be different, but the operation will be the same.
OSROSRhot raising OSRising OSRising OSRaising OSRising OSR

Bit instructions are very important when you are analyzing inputs and setting outputs. In the experiment, you will enter a program into the PLC trainer which will demonstrate some of the bit instructions that you have learned...
Always remember to refer to the PLC manufacturer's documentation for further details, limitations, and requirements for different instructions.

We are offline because we do not need to communicate with the PLC trainer yet. First, we need to write our ladder logic. Once we have created our ladder logic, we can send it to the PLC and test it...
The program that we are going to enter is shown below. Let's first look at what this program can do before we enter it into the APS software.

In rung 1, the eXamine If Closed instruction will look at bit 0 of input port 0 and return true or false based on its setting. Bit 0 of input port 0 represents one of the inputs of this particular PLC.
Input 0 is connected to the START switch on the 5050-1 process control board. When this switch is pressed, the bit will be set to one. When the switch is released, it will be set to zero.

If XIC returns true, both the operations after it will be performed. The first operation (OuTput Latch) will set output port module 0, bit 0, to high. LED 0 is connected to the output latch and will illuminate in response to the high. The LED will remain on until something else turns it off...

The second operation is the OuTput Energize instruction, OTE. This instruction will turn on LED 1 through output port module 0, bit 1, until XIC returns false. Then, output port module 0, bit 0, will be set to low again...
In other words, this bit stays high while the START button is pressed, which means LED 1 will stay on. LED 0 is off and will remain off when the START button is pressed and after it's released...

The second rung is very similar to the first one. The XIC instruction monitors input module 0, bit 1, which represents the STOP button on the 5050-1 card. When this switch is pressed in, output module 0, bit 0, which corresponds to LED 0, will be unlatched. This will turn LED 0 off...
Also, while the STOP button is pressed, output module 0, bit 2, which corresponds to LED 2, will stay high. Once the button
is released, output module 0, bit 2, will go low which turns off LED 2...
The third and fourth rungs both utilize the eXamine If Open instructions. These two rungs turn on and off LED 3 and 4 based on the position of the START and STOP buttons. They
are used to show the complementary action of the instructions XIC and XIO...
Whenever the START button is not being pressed, LED 3 will be on. When the START button is pressed, LED 3 will turn off. The same condition is true for rung 4, the STOP button, and LED 4.
